source.title: DAWN: Dynamic Adversarial Watermarking of Neural Networks
source.authors: Sebastian Szyller; B. Atli; Samuel Marchal; N. Asokan

record.file_problem: Text is the full paper; some PDF table layouts are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains surrogate networks on data containing deliberately mislabeled samples and measures accuracy on those samples, bearing on memorization of incorrect labels. It does not reproduce fully random labeling of the whole training set.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) for fitting arbitrary labels as rationale, but cited results are not extracted. Rows below are this paper’s own watermark-accuracy results on mislabeled trigger samples.
record.test_reason: DAWN uses memorization of deliberately incorrect labels as a watermarking mechanism and evaluates its embedding, verification and removal. It does not test complete random labeling, corruption-dependent optimization or generalization, unstructured inputs, or real-label versus noise learning dynamics. Its regularization experiments concern selected watermark triggers rather than fitting a randomly labeled training set.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct but incomplete. The authors conclude that DAWN watermarks all six tested first-order extracted surrogates while imposing little loss on the protected victim's utility. They acknowledge that suitable regularization can weaken embedding, and that double extraction or fine-tuning can remove watermarks while preserving utility when the attacker has abundant natural data. They also identify successful inference-noise evasion in two of six cases under an allowed accuracy-loss budget.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models on API responses with selected incorrect labels for dynamic watermarking and model extraction, rather than assigning completely random labels to the full training set. It cites the original claim as motivation.
record.method_sensitivity: Watermark accuracy varies by model, capacity, regularization method, and extraction attack; the paper reports lower watermark accuracy for some low-capacity and regularized settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The six extracted surrogates reproduce deliberately incorrect watermark labels with 71.17–100.00% accuracy in Table 6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small subsets of pseudorandomly mislabeled API responses can embed verifiable watermarks in models trained through PRADA or KnockOff extraction.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.1 and Table 3 show that watermark embedding depends on model capacity and regularization. MNIST-5L dropout reduces watermark accuracy to approximately chance while damaging test accuracy; other settings reduce watermark accuracy while retaining useful test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization and capacity choices can weaken selected-trigger watermark memorization, with model-dependent utility costs.

record.problems: Watermark results concern selected trigger samples with incorrect labels, not complete random relabeling. Table 6 provides no uncertainty estimates. The regularization sweep in Table 3 contains many flattened entries and is not exhaustively extracted here.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 reports extensive per-model, per-regularization, per-training-stage watermark and test accuracies, including low or reduced watermark fit in some settings. These are omitted because the flattened table layout and the 60-row limit make full model-condition-stage extraction lengthy; the study's explicit discussion notes MNIST-5L dropout can reduce watermark accuracy to approximately 10%, and several settings reduce it to 20–35%. Tables 7–11 concern watermark removal or inference/training perturbations, not additional fitting of random labels as specified by the claim.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, zero or near-zero whole-training-set error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Zero training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A corruption-fraction sweep from none to all, perfect training fit throughout, and steadily increasing test error toward chance.

Regularization's inability to prevent fitting a randomly labeled training set, data augmentation, and generalization after removing explicit regularization. Table 3 instead evaluates resistance to embedding a small watermark.
Relative learning order and training dynamics of real labels and noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope labels mistake untested claim components for demonstrated limitations. Table 3 is already declared in rows_left_out, so its omission is not a missing-result entry. Tables 9–11 interchange the GTSRB-RN34 and CIFAR10-RN34 baseline watermark accuracies relative to Table 6; R4 and R5 correctly reproduce their cited Table 6.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fitting a selected subset of mislabeled training samples, not completely random labels across the full training set; chance test error and unchanged training hyperparameters are not tested.
Uses a fixed watermark size of 250 in the robustness experiments and does not sweep corruption fractions from none to all or report steadily rising test error.
Tests weight decay and dropout for watermark embedding, but does not test data augmentation or whether removing regularization alone harms generalization on true labels.
